content: The studies reviewed included 11 cross-sectional and cohort studies involving a total of 39,050 patients. These studies evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of HPV testing and cytology for detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or higher (CIN 2+). The following findings were observed: 1. False Positives (FP): Patients incorrectly classified as having CIN 2+ were reported in 11 studies. The absolute difference in false positives was 64 more cases when using HPV testing compared to cytology. The quality of evidence for this outcome was rated as low due to serious limitations, including indirectness and imprecision. 2. False Negatives (FN): Patients incorrectly classified as not having CIN 2+ were also assessed in 11 studies. The absolute difference in false negatives was 28 fewer cases with HPV testing compared to cytology. Again, the quality of evidence was rated as low due to similar limitations. 3. True Positives (TP): HPV testing demonstrated a pooled sensitivity of 94% (95% CI: 89–97), while cytology (ASCUS) showed a pooled sensitivity of 70% (95% CI: 57–81). This indicates that HPV testing identified 24 more true positive cases per 1,000 patients compared to cytology. 4. True Negatives (TN): HPV testing had a pooled specificity of 90% (95% CI: 86–93), while cytology (ASCUS) had a pooled specificity of 95% (95% CI: 92–97). This resulted in 90 fewer true negative cases with HPV testing compared to cytology. 5. Colposcopic Impression: Colposcopy had a pooled sensitivity of 95% (95% CI: 86–98) but a much lower pooled specificity of 42% (95% CI: 26–61). This highlights its high sensitivity but limited ability to rule out disease in patients without CIN 2+. 6. Quality of Evidence (QoE): The overall quality of evidence for these outcomes was rated as very low due to significant concerns about study design, indirectness, inconsistency, and imprecision. Many studies relied on a single biopsy of abnormal lesions, and blinding of test results was often unclear. 7. Screen-and-Treat Strategies: Different strategies for managing patients based on HPV testing, cytology, and colposcopy were compared. HPV testing followed by cryotherapy or LEEP (loop electrosurgical excision procedure) was associated with lower cervical cancer mortality and incidence compared to no screening or cytology-based strategies. However, these approaches also carried risks of overtreatment, including unnecessary procedures and associated complications such as major bleeding, premature delivery, and infections. 8. Complications: Major bleeding was reported in 0.17% of patients treated with cold knife conization (CKC), while premature delivery occurred in 5% of women who became pregnant after treatment. Data on infertility risks following treatment for CIN 2+ were not identified. 9. Cancer Detection: HPV testing detected more cancers at first-time screening compared to cytology. The number of cancers detected was calculated based on pooled data from multiple studies, with HPV testing showing superior performance in identifying screen-detected cancers. 10. Assumptions in Modeling: The analysis assumed no cervical cancer or CIN 2+ in true negatives (TN) and false positives (FP). For false negatives (FN), a 90% persistence rate of CIN 2+ without treatment was assumed, with a 10% regression rate. Mortality rates from cervical cancer were estimated based on data from women with unknown HIV status. 11. Limitations: The wide confidence intervals (CIs) for sensitivity and specificity of cytology followed by colposcopy, as well as for true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives, may lead to different clinical decisions depending on the assumed confidence limits. Additionally, the lack of direct data for some outcomes and reliance on pooled estimates from observational studies further limited the strength of the conclusions. In summary, while HPV testing demonstrated higher sensitivity for detecting CIN 2+ compared to cytology, it also resulted in more false positives. The evidence supporting these findings is of low quality, and further research is needed to address the limitations and improve the reliability of these diagnostic strategies.
